I wish to refer to a matter in regard to which I asked the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce a question yesterday. Is the fixed price of wheat until August 31 applicable only to the wheat of last year's crop, or is it applicable to new wheat coming forward?
Old and new.

At what date did that
proposition take effect? I want to draw the minister's attention to the fact that on the 24th the cash price of No. 1 and No. 2 Northern wheat in Winnipeg was $2.40, No. 3 Northern, $2.38. In Minneapolis, No. 1 Northern, $2.60 to $2.65, and No. 2 Northern $2.55 to $2.60.

The order took effect, as far as the price and inclusion of the new crop is concerned, on the date of the promulgation of the order, somewhere between the 15th and 20th of the month. I forget the exact date.
It was the date I wanted to get.
My hon, friend will remember that I read the orders and they were placed on Hansard about ten days ago.
On the Orders of the Day:

I notice in the Citizen this morning a statement that Thomas Kelly who was sentenced to some two years and a half in the Stoney Mountain penitentiary, on the verdict rendered at the Manitoba Assize Court, has been given ticket-of-leave by the Minister of Justice. Some days ago I asked that hon. gentleman (Mr. Doherty) if any petitions had been received by the Department of Justice, and he answered in the negative, gentleman (Mr. Doherty) if any petitions since, and is there any correspondence in the matter to be laid on the Table of the House? If Kelly has been given a ticket-of-leave on account of his health, I ask that the medical certificates be laid on the Table of the House.
Hon. 'C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :	I think the hon. gentleman
must have misunderstood me, if he apprehended that I had said that there had been no petitions for the release of Kelly. Petitions were received at different times. Since the hon. member referred to the matter on a former occasion, it 'has been represented to us that Kelly's health was in such a condition that there was actual danger of death. We had previously received representations with regard to his health. Since he has been confined to the penitentiary it has been necessary to hold him under medical treatment all the time, and the penitentiary surgeon, who unfortunately died recently, some time ago expressed the decided

opinion that Kelly should be released.
I have not the dates of his last report on the subject, but 'I think it was in June. He had previously reported in April, .and I think even before that, expressing his opinion that Kelly should be released. His last Teport was to the effect that he would not take the responsibility of his being longer detained, and we caused Mr. Kelly to be examined in March or April, I think, by Dr. Lafleur, of Montreal, who, I think, the hon. gentleman knows, is a very eminent gentleman in his profession, and, as a consequence of his report, we did not feel justified in acting upon the Teport of the jail surgeon. But quite recently it was reported to us, as X have said, that the prisoner was in such a condition that there was danger of his death. Upon that information coming to us, which came through members of his family, who had been gathered at the penitentiary by reason of his critical condition, I caused the prisoner to be examined by Dr. Popham, of Winnipeg, a physician of very high standing, who,
I am quite satisfied, is above any suspicion of expressing an opinion other than his genuine professional opinion. He reported that he found Kelly in bed suffering from gastritis, with a very high temperature-I forget exactly what it was and rapidly losing in strength; also that Kelly had lost weight really to .an alarming extent, I cannot mention just now the number of pounds, and there was no prospect of improvement under existing conditions. Under those circumstances I felt that I should entirely fail in my duty if I did not recommend that Kelly should be transferred to a hospital, where he could receive proper treatment. I made that recommendation and a ticket-of-leave for that purpose was issued. Should Mr. Kelly recover, the question, of course, would remain open as to whether he should not be returned to the penitentiary, or whether further action should be taken. But certainly the circumstances left it beyond doubt, I think, that no other course was open to us that to allow this man to have the treatment that, upon high medical professional recommendation, was considered necessary for the preservation of his life

I rise to a question of privilege. I do not often refer to anything that I find in the newspapers, but when the newspapers get astray to the extent of $350,000,000, I suppose we ought to pull them up and put them right. I have been represented in the Ottawa Journal as saying that if the Canadian Northern Railway Bill went through it would increase the public debt to the extent of $800,000,000. I never made any such statement. I was replying to the statement of my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark), that the soldiers were doing a great deal of thinking, inferring that when they came home they would insist on some necessary reforms. I ventured to say in reply that when the soldiers went away the public debt of this country was $350,000,000, roughly speaking; that ,if we put this Bill through, the public debt when the soldiers returned would be $800,000,000, meaning that there would be an addition of $450,000,000, and not an addition of $800,000,000 as stated by the Journal. The other question was whether that debt was a net debt or a gross

debt. That depends largely on how you look at it. At present the road is not paying interest and running expenses, and I inferred that under public ownership it would not do any better, so that if the people of this country have to .tax themselves for the interest on the 3450,000,000 we might as well at once add that amount to our net debt, as that is what it would mean. All I have to say about the writer in the Journal is that if he read what was said in Hansard he either intentionally misconstrued what I said or else was too wooden-headed to understand plain English.

House again in Committee of Supply, Mr. Eainville in the Chair.
Department of Railways and Canals-Canadian Government .Railways, rolling stock, $25,000,000.

This vote is to. provide for the purchasing of fifty engines from the Montreal Locomotive Works-thirty Mikados at $48,750, ten Santa Fes at $56,000, and ten Pacifies at $47,300. Then there are to be purchased fifty locomotives from the Canadian Locomotive Works, Kingston, at $48,750. There are also 6,000 box cars, as follows:
1.000. 40-ton steel-frame box cars purchased from Canadian Car and Foundry Company at $2,417 each; 1,000, 40-ton steel-frame box cars purchased from Eastern Car Company at $2,417 each; 2,000, 40-ton steel-frame box cars purchased from Canadian Car and Foundry Company at $2,647.50 each; 1,000, 30-ton steel-frame stock cars purchased from Canadian Car and Foundry Company at $2,271 each; 1,000, 40-ton steel-frame box cars purchased from the National Steel Car Company of Hamilton at $2,647.50 each.
Then there are fourteen 10-wheel Chicago Great Western Kailway second-hand locomotives amounting to $4,748,700 for further purchase of rolling stock that may be required.
What does that rolling stock consist of?
Freight cars.
Is that for the Canadian Northern or only for the Transcontinental and Intercolonial?

What we purpose
doing is to use what is necessary on the

Government roads and then distribute the rest where necessary.

That means on the
Canadian Northern?
Yes.

Have those contracts
been already let in anticipation of this vote?

Contracts for 6,000
cars have been let.

When are deliveries to
take place?
They are all to be delivered before 1st February next. The deliveries are to start in October.

Have those cars been
ordered in Canada?
Yes.

What is the price of
a box car now, and what was the price before the war?
For the same style of car, the price before the war was about $2,200; the price now is $2,647.50.

Did I understand the
minister to say that a part of this rolling stock was intended to supplement the present rolling stock of the Canadian Northern?

I said that we would use what was necessary on the Government roads and then distribute the rest where it was most needed on the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific. There is a great shortage of equipment on all the railways.

The minister's present action is in accordance with the position taken by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) some two years (ago, that we should order more rolling stock. The minister has put off doing so to a very late date, and I question whether he will he able, in view of the difficulty of getting raw material, to secure delivery of those cars by the first of February. The minister states that he has purchased some secondhand rolling stock in the United States. From whom was that purchased, and what was the price per locomotive and per oar?
We purchased fourteen second-hand locomotives from the Chicago Great Western railway at $12,300 each, or about one-quarter of what we are paying now.

Can the minister give us the
dates of the contracts for these locomotives and cars?
The first contract was let in May; the last was let about a month or six weeks ago.
Were any second -hand cars bought in Chicago?

Not in Chicago, in
Ohio.
Mr. PUGSLgY:	What were they?

We bought 400 steel
cars in Ohio at $450 each. I am sorry to say we have received only 100 of them, and there is a little difficulty in getting the balance. '
In addition to that, some second-hand passenger cars were purchased?
That was last year.
No second-hand passenger cars are to be purchased out of this appropriation?
No.
Is there any provision for the purchase of second-hand passenger cars?
Not this year.

Is the Government
building any rolling stock in Canada? We have most excellent workshops at Moncton; we have workshops at Quebec in connection with the Transcontinental-
They are not equipped.

Then they ought to be
equipped. At Transcona we have very laTge workshops. Is the Government engaged in building any locomotives or cars at any of those places?

We are building some
vans at both Moncton and Transcona.
Those would be conductors' vahs.
Yes, and we are doing repairs. It is difficult to keep up with the repairs on the system at the present time.
WTiat are the Transcona shops being used for now?
For repairs, not only for the Government railways, but for the Grand Trunk Pacific.

It was rumoured some two years ago, or perhaps later than that,

that a portion of the Transcona shops had been leased to a company for the manufacture of shells. Is that correct?
Yes.
Are shells being manufactured there?
Yes.
Does that interfere with the construction of locomotives and cars?
No. ,
About what portion of the Transcona shops are being utilized for building these vans and for repair work for the railway, and what portion for making shells?
A very small portion is being used far making shells. I have not the exact floor space.
Who are the lessees of that portion of the Transcona shops?
A Montreal concern. I do not know who they are.
Was the contract made with the Department of Railways?
No, it was made with the Grand Trunk Pacific before it was taken over.
Who pays the rent and wnat rent is being paid?
I have not that information with me, but I will get it for the hon. member.
I am rather curious to know who the parties are who have leased those shops and the rent that is being paid.
The information was laid on the Table in a return last session.
I should' be glad if the minister lyould get it from his officials.
I will do it.

I think the committee should be informed as to how much of this large amount of rolling stock is required
by the present Government railways_the
Intercolonial and the Transcontinental. I understand from the minister that part of this rolling stock is to be used on the Government railways, and part distributed between the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific. That is a very general statement, and may cover the fact that possibly 50 or 75 per cent of this $25,000,000 
for rolling stock should properly be added to the liability the country is about to assume in respect to the Canadian Northern. The minister, I am sure, will be able to tell us what the requirements of the Government railways are, so that we may know jn fact how much of this amount is being added to the Bill for the Canadian Northern.

It has been estimated by my officials that we will need all the cars ourselves on the Government railways, with the exception of possibly two thousand	these two thousand together
with any others we may have to spare, will be used in helping out not only the Canadian Northern but other railways. The Grand Trunk, as everybody knows, is very short in equipment, as regards both power and cars. An arrangement has been made between' the railways of Canada and the coal shippers of the United States whereby cars bringing coal to this country will be returned to the United States empty. The shippers of stone and gravel in different parts of Ontario are in consequence unable to get cars, and they have been here asking us to buy equipment and lease it to the Grand Trunk.

I do not wish to criticise the minister for buying these cars; quite the contrary, rather I agree with the hon, member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) that it would have been sound policy to buy this rolling stock sooner. Nor do I find fault with the policy of leasing the rolling stock to railways that are not able to provide their own equipment. All I wanted to know was how much of this expenditure should be added to the bill for the Canadian Northern. My hon. friend says that two thousand of these cars will not be required on the Government railways. If the cars cost $2,500 apiece, I may be correct in saying that this expenditure of $5,000,000 should be added to what we are to pay for the purchase of the Canadian Northern. I am not finding fault with the minister for providing this equipment for the different roads, but we should be informed how much it will cost as regards the Canadian Northern and the other roads. *

The minister speaks of the distribution of cars among the different railways. I quite agree that that is desirable. I think it is greatly to be regretted that the Government waited till three years after the war before taking .any steps in this direction.
There is not a single year in which, we have not bought rolling stock.

The minister ought to have bought rolling stock. The Government roads and other railways have been continually short of equipment. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Poster), a few days ago, referred to the most admiralble arrangement that has been made in the United States, where the railways have joined together and appointed a small executive, which, so far as transportation is concerned, makes all the railways of that country, some eighty-five in number, into one system for all practical purposes. The executive has control of the distribution of the cars, and 'the minister stated that very satisfactory results had followed from that arrangement. But there was one thing he failed to point out, though I pointed it out my-self some few weeks ago, and that is that the railway companies were induced to take that action by the Government of the United. States. It was the Government of .that country that, immediately	on	the	breaking	out of	thewar, summoned in conference the presidents of all the railway companies of the United States, and it was	at	the	insistent	request	of
the Government that this arrangement was entered into. I am very sorry, and I think it is very much against the transportation interests of the country that the same thing was not done in Canada when the war broke out. The government railways, the Grand Trunk, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Canadian Northern, the -Canadian Pacific, and any other smaller railways-and there are some in Canada-should all have been parties to an arrangement Whereby rolling stock could be placed by a small executive where it was most needed in order to meet the transportation requirements of the country, just as is done in the United States. However, it is never too late to do good, and I am very glad that at last, following the example of the United States, the Government is moving along these lines, even if only a very short way.

I am sure my hon. friend has overlooked one fact, namely, that the railways in the United States are solvent. The railways now being operated by Mr. Willard are not railroads in the hands of receivers. If they were in the hands of receivers the conditions to which my hon. friend refers would not obtain. As the
Grand Trunk Pacific railway last year earned less money by operation than it required for the hiring of its equipment, and as the-Canadian Northern was behind from $5,000,000 to $7,000,000 in net revenue to supply its fixed charges, the difficulty of operating in the manner indicated by my hon. friend must be very apparent and very great, because each company is out now to get all the profit it can, in an endeavour to meet its fixed charges. And the competition that obtains here does not obtain to the same extent and in the same manner in the United States. There the presidents of the different roads got together, and Mr. Willard was appointed chairman of a small executive. Under his direction cars are allocated to certain lines for certain .purposes, but not to interfere with the revenues of the different roads. But where you have so much duplication, where two systems are not earning fixed charges, and the other system is earning enough to pay the fixed charges of both, the situation is difficult to deal with, unless the Canadian Pacific is willing to part with some of its money. It is perfectly obvious that you would have to take part of the net revenue of the Canadian Pacific Railway obtained from the carrying of traffic, passenger and freight, at fixed rates common to all roads as determined by the Board of Railway Commissioners, and pay it over to the other two roads to -make up their deficit. That is the position; it is very unfortunate, but that is the fact.

I think my hon. friend 'has exaggerated the difficulties. Jf the executive in the United States takes rolling stock from one road and sends it to carry the traffic of another, there would necessarily be allowed to the company whose cars were taken a reasonable per diem remuneration for the cars so used; and that is 'how it would work out in Canada.

How many of these six
thousand cars are being made by the Canada Car Company?
Four	thousand.

Who has the contract for
the other two thousand?

The	National Car
Company and the Eastern Car Company are making one thousand each.
I understood the minister to say that one part of the contract was let in May and another part about a month ago.
One contract was let in May, to the Eastern Car Company, and the other to the Canada Car Company.
Are any of the cars under that contract ready for delivery at the piesent time? Is delivery being made a:-the cars are built?
The first cars, will lie delivered in October.

I wish to '*evert to a discussion which I had with ibe minister some time ago in regard to the lifting of rails on the Grand Trunk Pacific west of Edmonton. We had somewhat warm words then, and the minister very strongly impressed upon the House and the country that the rails of the Transcontinental were of a certain size and boring, which obliged him to take rails from the Grand Trunk Pacific west of Edmonton, although it would have been more in accord with public policy if they had been taken from the Canadian Northern. I understand the Government has taken up the rails of the Grand Trunk Pacific and has replaced some of them with Canadian Northern rails, the reason being that although the Canadian Northern rails are of the same weight and quality they are bored somewhat differently and for that reason it was not advisable that they should be sent to England, inasmuch as they would have to be laid under fire, and there was a disadvantage in the possibility that the rails might not match. I think the minister made some remarks which reflected upon my patriotism and interest in the success of our endeavours in Europe, but of this I will not say anything further. I have a letter from a man who is employed in a railway battalion in France, and it may interest the House and the 'country to know what he has to say on this subject. He says:
The Huns left Bapaume on the 17th of March, and not only was the town wrecked but the railway was more than wrecked. What rails he left he blew up/at the joints, which broke the end of each rail. Where there was a deep fill it was mined and lifted out and the road bed was practically a line of shell holes. Well, we had a train of ammunition in on Easter Sunday and it was moved up in trucks. We had to use all kinds of rails, short and long, large and small. The engines here are not as heavy as the ones at home, so. we can use light rails, and the great, guns are mounted on thirty, wheels and reach over one or more raiis and some twelve joints in the car, so they play around the sharp curves as easy as a regular car, and as their heft is distributed over so much rail it allows us to use a light rail or anything we have. I was in the shops rebuilding fishplates to join up the different size rails. We had a lot of rails from England that have a ball on either side

and no base. They are set in castings called chairs. We joined up all this sort of steel and got the trains going and pushed the road on towards the front. When the train got in there was no limit to material. Rails poured in from everywhere. Ties and bridge timber piled up like small mountains. There was no lack of such material.
I think under the circumstances, and with that evidence, it will be clear that there was no warrant for the minister's suggestion that it was necessary to exchange the Grand Trunk Pacific rails for Canadian Northern rails or to take the Grand Trunk Pacific rails.

All I can say is that we followed the instructions received from the British Government. I think they know what they want. In any event, I am prepared to give them what they ask, as long as we have it.

The item under discussion is an item of $25,000,000 for the purchase of rolling stock. I think the minister exp'ained that a portion of this is to provide funds for the purchase of some 6,000 freight cars, the price for which is stated to be about $2,600 each, I believe. May I ask if that is the order that was given to Rhodes, Curry & Company?
They are the same as the Canada Car Company.
When is delivery of those cars to be made?

From October to 1st
February. They are all to be delivered by 1st Februray next.

My inquiry, a? the minister may surmise, is based on the fact that these are war prices. My recollection of previous purchases leads me to think that the prices now being paid are double or more than double what they were.
No, that is not the case.

If those deliveries were to run after the war, the purchase could not be justified as a good business transaction. However, if the whole 6,000 are to be delivered before February next, it is a different matter.

The contract is that
they shall all be delivered by February next. Of course, there are three different concerns building those cars. The Canada Car Company is only building 4,000, the Eastern Car Company 1,000, and the National Car Company 1,000.

, Mr. COPP: I would like to draw the attention of the minister to a question I put before'him when his regular estimates were under discussion, with regard to the relaying of the rails to the Sackville and Dorchester wharves. Since the matter was up before I have received a letter from a gentleman in Dorchester who is particularly interested in it. I will not place the letter on Hansard, but I would be glad to send it to the minister for his attention. This gentleman is manager of a large stone company down there which is using the wharf for the transportation of stone. He says " if some such thing as this is not done the Dorchester Stone Works Company will be put out of business." The stone is quarried and cut during the summer, and it is absolutely impossible to ship it until the rails are relaid.
Will my hon. friend tell me if they can get boats to bring the stone there now? I understand they cannot.

I am not sure. I simply mention this letter to bring the matter to the attention of the minister. There is a sketch attached to the letter showing that the relaying of about 200 yards of rail would be sufficient to obviate the necessity of hauling the stone over some very heavy hills.

Has the minister any
plans in regard to increasing the Tolling stock in the refrigerator service for the transportation of fish? This question was bi-ought to the attention of the minister by a committee of this House last year, and it was urged that something should be done. It was pointed out that the Intercolonial railway was not in a position to carry perishable products of that kind by express from the East to Montreal and Toronto. There is a special interest in the transportation of fish at the present time when it is proposed that there should be two meatless days every week. The cities of Ontario have to be supplied with fresh fish, I suppose, either from the Pacific ocean or from the Atlantic. The facilities are certainly not good at the present time. It is a reproach to the Intercolonial railway that, after it has been running for nearly half a century, it is not possible to-day to send a package of fresh fish in a refrigerator car from Eastern Canada to any of the cities in Ontario. If we wish to send a whole carload there are facilities for it either by express or by fast freight; but I am referring now to smaller packages for which there are no facilities in refrigerator
312*
cars. I do not know whether the minister is working out any plan to meet that want or not, but when we are embarking upon the expenditure of a large amount for rolling stock, I would like that matter to be kept in view.
We have ordered 100 refrigerator cars and I think they are delivered; if not they will be delivered before the end of the month.
Does this include the purchase of any private cars?
No.

I have seen in the press quite recently that different ministers have been obtaining private cars, and, among them, the hon. the Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid). He is the latest minister to have -a private car. I would ask if that car has been purchased and is being looked after by the Department of Railways and Canals, or whether it was purchased directly by the Department of Customs and is being looked after by the officials of that department?
He has no car. He uses a car once in a while the same as any other minister, but the car he uses belongs to the country and is controlled by the Government.
How many private cars does the Government have at the present time?

Six, including the
Governor General's car.
What officials in the service of the department does the minister consider entitled to private cars?
I do not know that any of the officials of the department use private cars except officials on the railway.
What officials on the railway are entitled to private cars?
Certain of them.

Does the minister think that in times like these, when the people are being urged by the Government to produce and save, it is right that the superintendent of a certain section of the railway should spend $150 or $200 a day of the country's money rolling around
4 p.m. in a private car when he could, just a-s well as the ordinary citizen, be carried in a Pullman. Private cars are attached to the ordinary trains

making them much' heavier and delaying ordinary passenger traffic. It is time that the department of railways should give this matter attention. It- is not fair to the country or the travelling public that an ordinary superintendent of the railway, who is neither a king nor a peer, should he entitled to this kind of entertainment with cooks, servants and everything that a millionaire could get by his money.

The hon. gentleman
certainly knows 'better. He is making statements that are nothing but foolishness. There is not a railway superintendent on any railway in the country who does not have a private car. It is his home, his office, his sleeping apartment, his everything, and it is impossible for a superintendent to do his work without one either on the Intercolonial or any other road in Canada. If the Government is going to be in the railway business it must follow the practice adopted on all railways.

I may be foolish and know nothing about railways, but I do know that we are told by members of the Government from the Prime Minister down that this . is a time -when public money should not be spent recklessly. I do not think it is a proper answer to make to an hon. member of this House, however humble he may be, that he is foolish and does not understand what he is talking about. I have travelled over the Intercolonial too much not to know what is going on. I think that the Minister of Railways owes ordinary courtesy to a member of this House who asks a question in good faith.
Have under-secretaries equally the use of private cars with members of the Government?
I think the under-secretary of one department has had a car once or twice.
Which department?
Militia.
When the minister said that the Government had six private cars he .meant, I presume, that they had six in addition to the cars which are used by officials at headquarters at Moncton?
Yes; these are official cars.
These six cars are just for the use of those whose headquarters are in Ottawa?
Two of them belong to the Governor General.

I do not think the minister quite apprehended my question. I asked him if the under-secretaries had equally the use of private cars with the ministers?
Mr. 'COCHRANE: I said one under-secretary had had one once.
To say that an under-secretary had one once is not an answer to my question. Assuming that an under-secretary desired the use of a private car, could he have the use of it?
Yes, if there was one available.
When an under-secretary wishes to travel in state and comfort, he has the right to use a private car if a private car is available?	.
Yes.
And the cost which is involved in the transportation of a private car is borne by the Government and not by the under-secretary?
Yes, and it is borne by every railway in the country, too.
Railways have not undersecretaries, as a rule, who travel in private cars.

Apparently the minister misunderstood the question asked by my hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr.- Carroll). He asked him as to the number of cars which were in use iby officials on the Intercolonial. I presume he misunderstood the question, because he answered by saying that the superintendents should have private cars. Inasmuch as we have the information in regard to the number of private cars kept for the use of the Government, it would be well that the committee should know how many private cars are in use by officials of the Intercolonial and what officials are entitled to the use of these cars.

The general manager, the general superintendent, and each of the superintendents have private cars. It is good business to give -them private cars, too. They do all their work on these cars; they live in them, practically. This is not a new system; it is the system that has been in use for years and years not only on the Intercolonial, but on every road in this country.

I am not raising the point as to whether it is good business or not.

How many district superintendents are there?
Four.
Who have private cars at Moncton? I am not in a position to speak positively, 'but I understood the general traffic manager also had a private car.
I do not think so.
He always used one. Mr. Tiffin had one.

In olden times, not
now.

I think the hon. minister said there were six private cars belonging to the Government. How many have we secured since the Government came into power?
Mr.	COCHRANE:	Two.Mr.	KNOWLES:	Is it permissible	for
a minister's private secretary to use a pri-cate car?

No, but the private
secretaries have a right to go with the ministers.

Mr.	COCHRANE:	I do not	know.Mr.	BURNHAM:	Are these	not office
cars?

This would be a good time
to obtain' further information as to the policy of the department with regard to private cars. Heretofore, we have had a certain number of Cabinet ministers, but the number has been increased from time to time until we have now, I think, sixteen. It is conceded that they have the right to use private ears when they desire to travel that way. A new policy has been adopted of appointing under-secretaries, and I should like to know if, when they desire to travel, they are to have the use of private cars at public expense quite irrespective of whether or not they are travelling on public business. The Minister of Railways stated on one or two occasions that the Under Secretary of the Militia Department travelled in a private car.
I should like to know if on any occasion the Under Secretary of the Militia Department desired to make a trip to the Maritime Provinces, would he, as a matter of right, have a private car at his disposal, and have the cost of transportation in that way paid by the Government?

The minister made the statement. I naturally thought that that implied that if the under secretary desired to use the car on public business he would have the right to it. I infer that the minister goes further, and that he means that the under secretary, no matter whether he is travelling on public, or private business, has the right to travel in a private car- and his family, of course.

Does the minister know whether any members of the Railway Commission of Canada ever go so far as to accept the present of a private car from an incorporated railway company while they are on personal trips, such as holidays?
I have not any information as to that. They have their own car, at any rate.
Would they have the right to have their own car hauled free on private business, such as a holiday trip?

The different railways furnish the Board of Railway Commissioners with passage all the time, and I think they are willing to haul the cars, whether on business or pleasure, but I have not any information on that point.
Will the hon. gentleman look into it, if he has time?
I do not know why I should.

I was going to give
the reason for my question. It may be foolish, but I must discharge my duty. I do not think the Board of Railway Commissioners should be under obligation to any railway. They are in a judicial position.	*
Perhaps a member of Parliament should not be under obligation.
Two blacks do not make a white.
We have the right to travel free by law.
Yes, and that is another matter.

The members made
the law, not the railways.

I may go a long way
with the minister, and I might say that the members, might for their own self-respect pay the money to the railway companies for fares, and if the people wanted to reimburse them, let them do so. I hold the view that the Board of Railway Commissioners should not accept any personal favours from any railway. They are adjudicating upon matters in which one of the contestants is the railway company and the other may be a comparatively unknown and obscure citizen. An official whose position calls upon him to discharge duties in an impartial manner should not be under the slightest obligation to either of the litigants. If my view commends itself to the minister and if he finds that the practice is what I have indicated. I think he should look upon it with disfavour. Will the minister look into the matter and give it consideration?

I do not think I will.
I do not think it is my business to look into it. I have perfect faith in the Board of Railway Commissioners, and anything they take in the way of transportation from the railways would not have much effect on them.

They are human, like
every one else. I am not going to attack them. They are not heTe, but, in defence of the public interest there should be rules laid down so that there would be no suggestion of anything like their receiving favours from the railways, I would go further, and although the reason does not apply so strongly, I would say that judges who are acting, where railways are litigants, should not accept favours. It is the constant duty of the Railway Commission to hold the scales of justice evenly between the railway companies and private citizens.

And it is the duty of legislators to legislate for the railways. You take a pass from the railway company, and still you are kicking.
{Mr. Knowles.]
No. I never took a pass, that I recollect.

The hon. gentleman
is the exception.

The point raised by the hon. member for Moosejaw is one that has engaged the attention of legislatures and Congress of the United States. The statutes of most of the western states prohibit any legislator from accepting transportation, and when I was entitled to transportation on some of the roads by reason of my professional engagements, I used to have to sign a statement that I was not a member of any legislature of any state through which the road in question passed. In most of the western states, if not all of them, there are now statutes absolutely prohibiting any member of the legislature from accepting transportation, and rendering liable not only the railway company which gives tile transportation but also the recipient as well. In the United States they have the Interstate Commerce Commission, which performs to some extent the functions of our Board of Railway Commissioners, and very drastic and extreme regulations have been passed by that commission. I quite agree with the hon. member for Moosejaw that we should enact legislation. It is not for the Minister of Railways to do it; it is for us here, and for the Railway Committee if they so desire in dealing with the Railway Act, to declare that no transportation shall be issued to judges, if you please, or to others. It would be competent, and probably not improper, for Parliament to declare that no public servant, and no one occupying the position of a judge in the cases mentioned by the hon. member for Moosejaw, should receive favours from railway companies. The same argument could he applied to telegraph companies, and in that case my hon. friend from Moosejaw could not be the recipient of any form of pass that would entitle him to free service on the part of the telegraph company or the railway. That is the point he is making, and if hon. gentlemen will read the volumes and volumes of discussion which took place in the United States until they reached the point they have now-attained, I think it will be found that the question is really worthy of consideration by Parliament. Not that I think it has any effect on the minds of the judges themselves; I do not think it has; but it leaves the public in the position of the poor litigant with the idea that he is being unfairly treated, and that men are biased

against him by reason of what they receive, which is a. bad feeling to have in the country. It will be remembered that before the irftroduction of the present Railway Act every member had an annual pass, and I believe the late Minister of Railways was right and the Government was right in declaring that every member of Parliament should have free transportation on the railways, in order to remove the possibility of it being said that a favour was being extended to one member by a railway company which was not extended to another, because in some instances, if a man became vigorous in his onslaughts against a railway company, that company claimed the right to withdraw his transportation. That was the evil aimed at by the present legislation, which I think is sound, unless1 you pass a statute prohibiting railways from issuing transportation to a member of any legislature. If members of Parliament are to receive free transportation, it must be by Act Of Parliament; if not, the railway companies must be subjected to heavy fines for issuing transportation to members.
As to private cars, the Canadian Pacific railway supplies each district superintendent with a small car. It is marked on the end "business" or "official." It is usually without a name and has only a number. That is a greater workshop than the room a man has in any terminal of the road. Counting uip the hours of the district superintendent-there are three districts centering in Calgary, and I have the facts from district superintendents-he spends more hours in his icar in a year than in his office and his home. Thfen you come to the divisional superintendent, and he has a car. His duty is to control not only one division but several. One division superintendent-they have now changed the name as between districts and divisions^-who is now assistant general manager qf eastern lines, one year showed me his mileage. He had travelled in a year more than the distance around the world, on his oar day and night. He could not do his business without that car. The business of the railway could not be done without these cars. If the Canadian Pacific Railway, in the pursuance of sound business principles, supplies officers with cars, I think that the country must do the same with its officers, or fail in its duty. The higher officials are supposed to use official cars on official business; but in practice, if an official of the Canadian Pacific railway wants to go on Ms holiday, he
takes his car with him. If Mr. Hall of Winnipeg wished to go the coast he would take his car, and if Mr. Tiffin, for instance, wants to go to St. Andrews he, of course, takes a car. It is one of the perquisites they enjoy. The salaries in this country are so insignificant as compared with those paid in other countries, that if you add the whole thing together, it is not a high salary for a railway man.
The Intercolonial salaries have become pretty generous.

The salary paid to Mr. Gutelius was $5,000 less than he now enjoys. He is employed on a shorter road. The Delaware apd Hudson took him over. There is no reason why I should not tell this story to illustrate the attitude of public men towards these matters. There was once a prime minister of Canada who conceived the idea that he would like to have great business men operating the Intercolonial and he suggested to the greatest living railway man then in Canada the necessity and the desirability of getting these men. He said: You know I would not mind paying $5,000 a year for such a man. That distinguished railway man replied: If you will give me a hundred of them at that price I will take them to-morrow, because you cannot get railway men for $20,000 a year or $25,000 a year. The president of one road in this country, who is now dead, was employed by the Southern Pacific at $55,000 a year, as was made known in certain threatened ligitation. That was under the late Mr. Harri-man. It is not uncommon to see the president of a railway receiving $100,000 a year. That is a large salary, hut if we are to conduct business in this country-and we are going to have now a very large mileage; we shall probably shortly see operating 15,000 miles of rails- we must supply our officials with the same sort of accommodation as men in similar service on other railways enjoy. And we must pay salaries suitable to men who assume such large responsibilities. We cannot get away from that. It its not pleasant to contemplate, but it must (be done. I have thought it unfair for members to go into the back sections of the country and complain of the payment of these salaries. One is no better than the other. If we were in opposition and you were in power we would probably be doing the same thing.
I think the hon. gentleman should speak for himself.

I am glad that I am not able to -speak for my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), because I should be sorry to think that I would give expression to some of hi-s ideas. Human nature is human nature, and those in opposition are necessarily making capital against the Government of the day; but it is fair to say that we -should educate the people of this country into the belief, even in the country districts, that men discharging large responsibilities for the Government must ibe paid what they -are paid by private enterprise, and that the same facilities that are provided for the conducting of private business must be provided to carry on the public business. To point out that this man has a private car and some one else has some other kind of car, serves no useful purpose. The official car is useful for the proper discharge of the duties of the officials, and I think that the House should agree in that view and let it be understood that, so f.ar as we are able, we propose to put this country behind our servants, because they are our servants, for the purpose of doing the best that is possible for the country. One, of course, expects these discussions. They are always incident to the passing of estimates, but I do not think they serve any useful purpose.

I am inclined to think my hon. friend is encouraging the establishment of an era of extravagance in the public service. Take the manager of the Intercolonial. There has been no better manager, no more successful or satisfactory manager, than Mr. Pottinger, and Mr. Pot-tinger's salary, I think, during the thirty-five or iforty years he was connected with the railway, never exceeded $6,000 a year. When the Minister of Railways came to -appoint a manager he took Mr. Gutelius, who. I am satisfied, had never received over $10,000, and gave him a salary of $20,000 a year.
Mr, COCHRANE:	.Another road took
him at $25,000.

That may be. Perhaps there may be reasons. That road desires intimate connections with the Intercolonial. That -road has an opportunity to get traffic originating .in northern New Brunswick, of getting the traffic between the Intercolonial and New England points.
The Delaware and Hudson does not even touch it.

In connection with the
Quebec Central?
My hon. friend's geography is as bad as his facts.

Perhaps I am wrong,
but, at all events, we know that Mr. Gutelius never gave the same satisfaction-nothing like the same satisfaction to the public -as Mr. Pottinger gave.

Mr. KY'TE: Not as well.

not have the s:ame wrecks on the Intercolonial either-I say it advisedly

that we have had since Mr. Gutelius became manager. This Government has certainly entered upon an era of extravagance. All their officials are -receiving much higher salaries than were paid previously. I think that Sir Collingwood Sehreiber never received, during all the years he served under the late Government, upwards of $6,000 a year, although he was one of the best railroad engineers in the country and occupied the position of deputy minister, and chief engineer oif the Government system of railways. I do not think that in this country, it is necessary to give these extravagant salaries. I believe good men-the very best men-can be secured to perform the duties of these positions just as satisfactorily as these high-priced men, for salaries not very much higher than those that have been paid during the last fifteen or twenty years.

Inasmuch as the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) said that this matter was raised for political purposes, I desire to say that in that respect I plead no-t guilty. When an estimate like this is under discussion, hon. members are surely justified in asking whether any of the money is to be used for the purchase of private ears or not. The Government must not -be too touchy in regard to questions that are asked. We are asking questions in order to get information to which we have a perfect right. The number of private cars this Government is purchasing may be^ quite justifiable. The question is whether it is a matter of economy for Government officials to have private cars or not. If it is, then they should have them, but the number of pri-
[Mr. Oliver.!

vate cars may increase so as to become a nuisance. As one of my hon. friends on this side of the House said, these private cars are a great- inconvenience to the ordinary traveller on a railway. Not long ago I was travelling on the Canadian Northern to Toronto, and I wanted to make connections through Toronto to Winnipeg.
I found three private cars attached to the train. There was no need of those three cars at all; two of them were not occupied by the men who owned them. That, of course, was their business, and not mine, as the railway was not a government-owned line. The private car question, like any other question, is one that is quite justified so far as it is reasonable, but beyond that it becomes an abuse. When we have every parliamentary under-secretary running around the country in a private car, and any man on the railway commission sending out a private car with his wife and children to the seaside, that is a thing that should be stopped; it is vicious at the foundation; it is a loss of economy, and it has a bad influence on those receiving favours who should not accept them. I do not know why the minister said so much about hon. members of this House using passes. I suppose he meant our Tailway certificates under the Railway Act. I have travelled in -that sense on what he calls a pass. What I had in mind was the real pass. The minister surely did not mean to suggest that I had bothered him for passes, because I never did so. I never used any on his railway, either for myself or any one else. If my wife got one, I promise the minister I will send it back.
I was not^alluding to that.
The minister spoke as though he meant that I was trying to get passes.

Canadian Government Railways-purchase of steamers "McKee" and "Drummond," $1,020,000.
Will the minister explain this item?
They are two steamers we bought for the purpose of carrying coal from Sydney to Levis. One was bought for $515,000, and the other for $505,000. They have been on that work ever since.
Were they purchased in England?
No, in this country.
Are they second-hand steamers?
Yes. One was bought from the Algoma Central Company and the other from the company of which Mr. James Playfair is president-I forget the name of the company.
What, is the tonnage and the age of each steamer?
They were built in 1908. The tonnage is 3,400 tons.
They are carrying coal for use on the Intercolonial?

Yes.
Canadian Government Railways-to provide for building of two wooden ships, $600,000.
Will the minister explain this item?

We let contracts for two wooden ships to be built at North Vancouver, one contract to Wallace Shipyards, Limited, and the other to Harrison & La-mond, of Vancouver. The price was $230,000 in each case. Those contracts were let some time ago, but both firms cancelled them, refusing to go on with them. They claimed that the price was altogether too low. We have not made any other arrangements for the construction of these ships since then, but we hope to be able to get two boats. The idea was to put on these two boats to run between-Vancouver, Halifax and St. John, and also down to Bermuda.
Were tenders called for the vessels?
We asked for tenders from the different shipyards, and these firms signed contracts, but they have since cancelled them and refused to build the ships.

If it is decided to go on with the construction of -these vessels, I hope the minister will call for tenders in a public way, instead of inviting tenders from the owners of a few shipyards. In that way the East will have an opportunity of . tendering as well as -the West.
What is the tonnage to be?
It is 2,500 tons each. Mr. PUGSLEY: What power would they have?
Gasoline engines.

That is the Diesel engine, I suppose?
Mr. COCHlRANE: Oil engines. They will use sails as well.
Is the minister now anticipating that there will be an increase in cost which will bring the total up to $600,000?
They won't take them on any other terms except cost plus ten per cent.
Is there any information as to the standing of these firms? Had they built many ships before taking this contract?
The Wallace Shipbuilding Company have had several contracts.
Is that the firm Mr. Bowser is a director in?
I do not know.

I am informed he is.
Would they not have to put up a deposit on a contract like this?

They refused to put
up a deposit.
The contract was entered into by the Government without a deposit?
Yes,

Is it not unusual for
the minister to invite people to enter into a contract and for the contract to be let without any deposit being made?
Yes.
May I not get a promise from the minister that if he goes on with the construction of vessels he will call for tenders on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts?
I think that is a fair proposition.

If I remember correctly, Mr. Bowser at the time of the election was making considerable political capital out of the fact that he had arranged for the carrying on of this industry in British Columbia, and he himself was a director of this company.
I have never heard that in any shape or form.

As I understand it,
these vessels are intended to ply from At-
lantic ports like St. John and Halifax in winter, and Montreal in the summer-
Not from Montreal.

From Atlantic ports, we will say, and to pass through the Panama Canal on to the Pacific coast, making regular voyages between Eastern and Western Canada via the canal. So there is no reason why tenders should not be called for on both the Atlantic and Pacific coasts.
That is true.
What is the financial standing of this company? How was it they were let off so easily? How much paid-up capital have they?
I do not know.
Does the minister mean to say that he entered into a contract vdthout any depo'sit being made, and without inquiring into the financial standing of the companj''.

We were perfectly safe without a deposit, because we were to pay them on progress estimates, and we would have had a capable man there to report to us from month to month the progress they were making. So it was not necessary to get a deposit.

I wish to respectfully criticise the minister's view. If the public service demands that there should be ships, the public service demands that a contract should be entered into which there is reasonable ground to believe will be carried out. If we need ships, we should not play with the business. In this case, certain men in a certain place had the option of going ahead with a contract or throwing it up. If they saw they could make a profit they could go ahead, and if, after looking into the 'matter Carefully, they thought they could not make a profit, they could throw up the contract. If the minister lays that down as the established policy of the Government, even with the poor financial head that I .have I could be a millionaire in a very short time. I could simply pick and choose between the contracts, going on with this one here if I could make a profit, and dropping that one there if I could not make money on it. If the minister never bothered to enforce the contract it would be nice pickings. I think we have here a dangerous precedent, which is not altogether unlike the principle laid down in Winnipeg, where a minister, finding that the contractor had tendered for a little less

amount than would see him through, paid the difference.
But I have not.

This is just the reverse of that. In this case, the man is let off without being called to account. If it happened that the figure was one which subsequent fluctuations of the market with regard to labour and material justified him carrying on, he would have the option of making a very profitable deal with the Government. On the other hand, he could never lose, because if the market fluctuated against him he could throw up the contract. It is altogether to the disadvantage of the Government to do business in that way, and I wish to place myself on record *to that effect.

In justice to the minister and to the firm who failed to carry out their contract, it should be pointed out that just subsequent to the letting of this contract the Munitions Board entered into the business of building wooden ships in British Columbia and other parts of Canada and secured practical control of the material entering into the building of ships. There were only a limited number of mills in British Columbia capable of sawing the timber necessary for certain parts of these ships, and the Munitions Board immediately arranged for the control of the output of these mills, with the result that many shipbuilding firms were unable to get material for their private work or for work in connection with Government contracts.

Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that the Munitions Board deliberately interfered with the securing of supplies by these shipbuilding-firms who were going to build for the Government? Or did the board incidentally and accidentally take the material away from them?

The hon. gentleman's
word " deliberately " implies malicious intent.

Let us say, forseeing
the results.

In any event, the results were the same. The Munitions Board found, and it has been found, I think, in the United States in the construction of wooden ships there, that the only satisfactory basis on which to lot the contracts is, cost plus a percentage. The fluctuation in the price of materials makes it impossible to gauge the price with any accuracy. The Wallace firm entered into this con-

tract because it already was constructing ships for a private concern-the Brown-Oarruthers group, who were building under a British Columbia law which g^ve them a bonus. By the time the negotiations with the Wallace firm were completed, the Munitions Board had entered the field and materials had risen in value to an enormous degree, and it would have resulted in very serious loss to the Wallace firm if the Government had insisted on the exact terms of the contract. I do not think any member of this House desires to take advantage of a commercial firm because of abnormal conditions. I would point out that, having in mind such a case as this, the British Government clothed itself with statutory power to enable it to allow a contractor to abandon his contract without loss, if he could show that he had to abandon it on account of the peculiar conditions arising out of the war.
That is not the case here.
We have not such a law here, but it is a very reasonable precedent to follow.
Those are not the circumstances here at all.. The minister cancelled the contract without knowing anything about it. He knew nothing about the financial standing of the company.
He is one*of the wisest ministers here, and I think he knows pretty well what he is doing.

Perhaps he was guided by the wise head of the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) who knows the right thing to do from a political standpoint when it is necessary. I would presume that my hon. friend from Vancouver had suggested to these gentlemen: I will see the minister and get him to let you out, and then you can get a contract at cost plus ten per cent.
"Mr. COCHRANE: That is absolutely untrue.
It is absolutely without foundation.
We have ten plus in the estimate all right.
Order.

The original contract
was for $460,000 and we find an estimate now for $600,000, so the minister has the ten plus in his mind.
I certainly have not. I refused to do it.
Then the minister was requested to do it by my hon. friend?
No, not by my hon. friend; by the people themselves, and by the board of trade out there; and I refused to do it.

I think it is a peculiar condition of affairs that the minister should voluntarily allow a contracting firm which engaged to build two vessels for the Government and which is under legal obligation to carry out its agreement to abandon its contract. It is evidently a very reliable firm, otherwise it would not have contracts with the Imperial Munitions Board. This is such a peculiar condition of affairs that the minister should give some explanation to the House, and I think he should bring down the contracts and the correspondence before he asks the committee to pass this item. Of course, it is all very well for us to show our sympathies, but still a contract is a contract, a bargain is a bargain. This strong financial company undertook to build those vessels, and entered into a binding contract. The minister had so much faith in them that he did not require them to put up a deposit, as he always does and as every minister does in respect of public works, which deposit would be forfeited if the contractor failed to carry out his contract. The minister chose to trust them, and he took their contract. They are bound in law to carry it out. The minister has seen fit to release them from this contract, and he finds now that he will have to pay a very much larger sum in order to get the vessels built, and is providing in his Estimates a very muck larger amount than the original contract called for. I think under those circumstances the minister should not ask the committee to pass this item until the contract and the correspondence are before us. I was greatly surprised at the statement of my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) that the Munitions Board has taken charge of the output of the mills. That is not what they do, according to the information given me by the director of the Munitions Board. Such a thing as that was not suggested. It is only that they require to know that the contracting firm will have a reasonably satisfactory opportunity of securing timber; but that the Imperial Munitions Board commandeers the output of any mills or any manufacturers of lumber is something I do rot believe.

I did not make that
statement.

Yes, my hon. friend said they had taken charge of the output of the mills thereby preventing the Wallace Shipbuilding Company from carrying out its oontract with the Government. I was greatly surprised to hear that statement because it is entirely contrary to what I understood has been the practice of the Munitions Board. In the city of St. John a contract was given by the Munitions Board for the building of two vessels, and the contractors got their timber where they could or where they pleased. The Munitions Board does not undertake to supply timber. The contractor has to supply it himself, and I am quite satisfied, unless my hon. friend ie able to assure the committee to the contrary, that the matter of securing timber is a matter entirely up tp the contracting firm. If the Wallace Shipbuilding Company has taken a contract from the Munitions Board at cost plus, under which they are absolutely sure of getting the cost of building and ten per cent, I am quite sure it is they and not the Munitions Board who control the output of. those mills and that they have voluntarily taken a more profitable contract and given up the contract they had with this Government, and the Government has voluntarily released them.

The Wallace shipyards
have no contract from the Munitions Board for wooden ships. They had contracts for steel ships, and they have already launched one or two. They had contracts which, I think, are about completed now from a private firm for wooden ships. As to the Munitions Board commandeering the lumber, I never made any such statement. What I said was that when the Munitions Board entered the field, before the construction of those vessels commenced, they arranged for the output of certain mills which were the only mills able to cut certain long timbers required in the construction of those vessels.
Do I understand they arranged with the mill- owners?
Yes,

Under contract with the millowners?
Mr. 'STEVENS: I do not know whether it was under contract, or how it wras done. They arranged with the millowners so that

they controlled the full amount of the output. Those mills are cutting to capacity, not only for British Columbia shipbuilding, hut for shipyards in Eastern, 'Canada as well.
