remember once a lawyer in New Brunswick continued to argue after the magistrate had adjourned the court. He said: " Am I addressing an adjourned court?" The magistrate said: " You certainly am." If that applies, we .have been addressing the committee upon items long after they have been passed. I think you had better reverse your judgment, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I cannot. The resolution has already passed, and is marked so.
That cannot be.

My hon. friend had better let it go as passed. He knows he is only doing a lot of very nice and skilful feeling. He has all the information his head can hold, and more than he can digest. He will get the contracts and the correspondence, and then if he wants to raise a row about it he can do so. But, what is the use of holding up such a very large item as this for a little information with reference to a contract?
The $25,000,000 item has been passed.

The resolution can only be passed as a whole, and the Chairman seems to have taken it that it was passed, and so marked it. My hon. friend who is in the Chair now cannot go back on what he finds in the record. My hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) will make it easy for the Chairman who was, and for the ' present Chairman, if he will simply allow the item to pass as the committee understands it has been passed, and he will get the information lateT.

I would like very much to oblige my right hon. friend, but at the same time there are certain rules of procedure which we must follow. Take, for instance, the Public Works item; he will find a hundred sub-items under one general beading. The practice is always to>
take them sub-item by subiitem and each one is passed separately. The mere fact of the passing of one sub-item does not mean that all are passed. If the chairman has got it wrong, we must get him right. My right hon. friend asks us to treat as passed a subitem that has never been under consideration at all.
You have been talking about it for over half an hour.

About the question of
ships?

Yes.

Mr.^PUGSLEY: We were, but the chairman has brought us up with a round, short and sharp turn, and he tells us that we are out of order and that all these items have been passed because we considered this one sub-item. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) speaks of this as a small thing. Six hundred thousand dollars a small thing? My right hon. friend has become so accustomed in recent months to thinking in millions, and hundreds of millions, in connection with the Canadian Northern railway and other matters that this item of $600,000 is a mere bagatelle, a fleabite. The difficulty about this matter is that if the Minister of Railways -gets all his items through we may not see him again during the session. The session cannot last much longer now.
I think I have been here pretty regularly during the session.

Yes, my hon. friend
has. but he has been waiting to get his Estimates through and when he gets them through we may not see him again. It is always objectionable to allow an item to go through before important papers and contracts have been brought down. When I was Minister of Piublic Works the present Minister of Trade and 'Commerce would not allow me to get a vote through for a public building until I had brought down all the plans. I remember that on one occasion I had to bring down a cartload of plans prepared by the different architects and lay them on the Table. He seems to have changed his ideas as to the proper thing to do. I leave it to him whether it is unreasonable, to ask that we should have the contract. This is a most extraordinary situation. I do not believe there is another minister who would assume for a moment that the committee would absolve him from blame in having relieved a substantial firm from a binding contract or would permit him to get the item passed without giving the House the contract and correspondence which, in his opinion, warranted him in taking 5 p.m. such an extraordinary course. I appeal to my right hon. friend- my economical and prudent friend, a man who was supposed to be the watch-dog over the actions of his colleagues, the one man who was supposed to be in the past extraordinarily economical, who watched every penny of public money to see that it was not wasted-to say whether the action of the minister (Mr. Cochrane) is justifiable or not. Here my right hon. friend is face to face with the fact that this Government fMr. Cochrane.]
has thrown away $100,000 of the money of the people and has relieved a perfectly substantial shipbuilding firm from the performance of its contract when the minister knows that he will have to pay $100,000 to have that contract carried out.
He has not to do anything of the kind.
He may al*andon it altogether. I assume that when the minister asked for the money last year he did so on the understanding that it was in the public interest that these ships would be built.
I did not ask for it last year. This is the first time I have asked for it.
Or the year before?
No, never before.
Yes.
No.
Yes, last session, the Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid) who was acting for the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) asked for it.
He did not ask for anything for shipbuilding.
Yes.
No.
I very distinctly remember the statement that we were going to acquire two vessels for the purpose of carrying freight between the east and the west of Canada.
That was early this session.
The matter came up this session? *

It came up early in the
session in the budget debate.

Then the position is
that the minister entered into a binding contract on behalf of the Government for two ships without any vote from Parliament?
Yes.
That strikes me :is even more reprehensible.
All right, but my hon. friend carried on the same practice.

No, never; that would
be an unheard of thing when the late Government was in power. Did the minister, without any vote of Parliament, actually

enter into a contract in which he pledged the people to pay $460,000 for two ships? Is that what the minister says? Yet he says that we must pass this item and he refuses to give us any information.
Did not the Government of which you were a member enter into a contract for the construction of the Transcontinental railway without the consent of Parliament?
No; that was subject to the approval of Parliament.

Yes, but you entered
into, the contract before you submitted it to Parliament.

No, it was subject to
the approval of Parliament. That is often done. The Government of Sir John Macdonald entered into a contract for the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway but it was subject to the approval of Parliament.
This is subject to the approval of Parliament too.

Not at all. Does the
minister say that the contract is subject to the approval of Parliament? What does the minister say about that? He says nothing. Under these circumstances I think the contract really had better be brought down before the vote is passed.
I am willing to bring the contract down.

Bring it down before we
pass this vote?
No, why should I?

Why should you not?
We are here acting for the people of this country. We have evidence before us that the minister without any authority from Parliament, entered into a contract which while it was binding on the Crown, was not binding on the Wallace Shipbuilding Company under which they pledged themselves to build two ships for $230,000 each, or $460,000 for both.
We will let the item drop if you like.
I would not like to have you do that.
You cannot have every thing your own way.

I do not have many things my own way; it is not often that I
can persuade the minister to do anything like that. Perhaps after all the minister had better drop it. In war times we should not spend money unless it is necessary. It would be a very good idea to drop it. But I do not ask him to do that if he will bring down the contract.
I will bring it down.
Bring it down before we pass this item.
No, the item is passed. 1 will bring down a copy of the contract on Monday.
Before this item passes?
No, the item is passed.
I must differ from my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have to insist that this*item is passed. That is what I find before me. If the ^minister and the committee are willing that the discussion should go on, I have no objection.
This item was not passed. You were not here, Mr. Chairman, but everybody who was here knows that it was not passed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: These are the resolutions, and a resolution can only be put in this place after it is carried. The items are discussed, the resolution is put before the committee and is carried, and that disposes of it.
That never was done.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is what the record shows. '

There is another matter requiring further consideration. That is the standing of the Wallace Shipbuilding Company. I have a recollection that the corporation and the personnel of that company cut some figure in British Columbia politics during the period of the provincial election a year ago. I think it was stated in the press at the time that this company, which had had a corporate entity for some years, had not done any business, but suddenly became revived during the progress of the provincial election campaign and my recollection also is that ex-Premier Bowser appeared as a director of that company, and, inasmuch as that company purported to do business with the provincial government, ex-Premier Bowser had to retire from the directorship. I recollect having obtained that information from a perusal of

the press of British Columbia a year ago, and I think it would be well if the minister would give the committee some information as to the financial standing and the responsibility of that company, as well as the names of the directors, with whom the Government purported to do business under the contract referred to.

I think there is no doubt this item is not carried. We all understand it. On the succeeding page you will find bracketed together perhaps a dozen items, and the clerk runs them off one at a time. It does not follow that, because the first of those items is passed the last one is passed, nor does it follow in this instance, that because two items are passed,, the third item is passed. The committee assented, after a discussion not at all unreasonable, to the $25,000,000 rolling stock, and the item we now have before us is to provide for the building of two wooden ships. There is no minister whose estimates I would more willingly expedite, than those of the Minister of Railways. I like the way he administers his department. I think he administers it, on the whole, pretty fairly, and in a manly way; but in this instance I feel that he has information in his possession that we should have before we consent to this item. In the first place, he entered into a contract before Parliament authorized the expenditure of the money, which, in itself, is an un-usal and abnormal way of doing business. The normal way is that the expenditure is first authorized and the money voted by Parliament and then the minister is entrusted with the details of making the necessary contract. ' In this instance, the minister has taken upon himself to anticipate the approval of Parliament, an unusual position, and, therefore, not one in which we are to be less careful than usual, but more careful, and the minister should be the last to ask us to do anything which might be approaching a loose way of doing business. If I were to undertake the responsibility of acting in .an emergency for a principal I should think that was the very case where the fullest disclosure should be made to the principal and I should not say to him: "Here, you ratify that, and when I get ready I will bring down the reasons which compelled me to take the course I took." I think the unreasonableness this afternoon is not on this side of the House in asking that all these things be disclosed to us before we ratify what our agent has done, because the minister, after 
all, is the agent of Parliament in the expenditure of money. More than that, there are the very exceptional circumstances under which the contract was allowed to lapse; there must surely be some further explanation of that. The explanation given by the hon. member for Vancouver is no explanation at all. Let us suppose that the condition of .affairs had been reversed, and that the price, instead of proving non-attractive, had proved very attractive to the contractors, would they have excused, forgiven and released the Government? Are we handling immense sums of the people's money so as to give the person at the other end every favour and consideration? Would the minister do that if it were his own business in Sudbury, Sault Ste. Marie, Toronto, or anywhere else? No, he would not. If he had taken his chances on the rise or fall of the market, on the increase in the supply or demand of an article, and the party at the other end of the contract, with his eyes wide open, had taken his chances, if the developments in that commodity had been in favour of the minister's end, so that he found his bargain a profitable one to him, he would be the last man in the world to release the man at the other end. He would say: " Some day I will get stuck myself; it will be all in a life time. You take your medicine now and I will take mine at some other time." There should be some further explanation than what has been given as to why the Government released this company in such a very easy way. No reason was suggested until the hon. member for ' Vancouver strolled into the Chamber. He had so plausible good-natured, calm an explanation, like pouring oil on the troubled waters-and yet when you come to examine it, it does not amount to anything. He says that the Munitions Board and the Government wanted something to be built which required long timbers and the demand for long timbers was increased and while nobody controlled .the material-the Munitions Board did not commandeer it- yet by some chance those who had the material saw an opportunity of making a better deal with the Munitions Board, and the contract was allowed to lapse. But wThat is the serious aspect of it all? It is this-that in .this great struggle in which we are engaged it was found, that it was necessary that we should have wooden ships, and yet, instead of having them built, the time in which they might have been built has been allowed to slip away.

And the minister gives us no explanation for the great delay that has occurred because the whole contract has lapsed. It is not merely the money consideration, the question of time is even more important. All these weeks and months have slipped away, and we are without that thing we need, namely the wooden ships for our transportation. We must presume it was necessary to have them, and if it was necessary to have them, then time must have been the essence of that very necessity; and I say the minister, instead of asking us to pass this item with our eyes shut, should be the very first to say "There will be the fullest explanation upon it before the people's representatives are asked to pass this item."

There is a very important principle involved for the protection of the committee in the suggestion made 'by the hon. gentleman that because you find the name of the chairman to this resolution you are going to treat it as adopted. I have	the votes and proceedings
of yesterday, and the resolution is not in the records as adopted, and it has not been adopted to-day. I have been here, and hon. gentlemen opposite have been here, ever since the House opened at three o'clock. My right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Railways, and other gentlemen on the other side, have been here. The resolution has no date. The chairman has simply .signed it, I suppose in anticipation of the fact that it might be adopted. These items have .been under discussion to-day, and the only items which have been passed are the two first, one for the purchase of rolling stock, which we discussed for half an hour and more, and the other for the purchase of the steamer McKee and Drummond. We have now reached the third item, and it has not .been declared passed. As one member of the committee, I insist that it has not been passed, and we have a right to. discuss it.

I think what
has taken place is what might very naturally take place. The chairman read the resolution which covers three items. There was a fair discussion on the principal item, a short discussion on the next, and there was .some talk on the third. Several times hon. members would .say "carried," "carried." and then some member on one side or the other would rise and follow out the item still further; Although we have said "carried" the chairman waited until

Mr. PUGSLEY; He never said "carried" as to the third sub-item.
I do not know about that. The Chairman evidently understood it was carried and so marked it.
He does not mark it "carried," he simply signs it.
There was no effort to crowd the vote through the committee in any way.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I
should be sorry if I had made any mistake, but I have been in the habit of considering each page placed before me as an item. In the resolution on the page before me, which calls for the vote of $26,620,000, there are the three items. That is resolution 437, and that was the resolution before the committee.
But you were taking it sub-item by sub-item.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Unfortunately that
was not done; I read the three items together, and when I said "carried" I referred to item 437.
But in the Public Works Estimates given on page 11, item 457, there are twenty sub-items. You call each subitem.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would read all the items, and if any hon. member asked for information, for instance about line 4, I would stop and permit him to ask for that information, and I would call "carried" when all the items in the resolution had been discussed in that way.

I appeal to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that there is no reason for this discussion. The practice has always been that the resolution is called. It may be composed of several items, absolutely disconnected. Here are three. These are taken one by one. We were on the third, which was being discussed when the Chairman left the Chair and the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. D. Stewart) took the Chair. The Chairman (Mr. Rainville), assuming it would be carried without further discussion, marked it. But the invariable practice is, when you have a resolution of several items, to take up each sub-item, and the resolution is carried when all are agreed to. The minister will agree on that point.

My right hon. friend is correct. This is merely a mis-



understanding, and I am sure that, if It is the desire of hon. gentlemen, the Chairman will be willing to consider this item as being allowed to stand.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If it is the pleasure of the committee, I have no objection.

I thought it would interest the minister to know that a telegram came to Ottawa to-day saying that a car of fish supposed to be shipped by the Maritime Fish Corporation could not be shipped owing to lack of equipment on the railway. The car was intended for Toronto.
Who received the telegram?
Matthews-Black well, Limited.

I have not heard of that before.
Railway subsidy-to provide amount required to be paid for the Quebec, Montmorency and Charlevoix Railway, the Quebec and Saguenay Railway, and the LotbiniSre and Megantic Railway, and' for the equipment, appurtenances and properties used in connection with such railways, to be acquired under the authority of a statute passed at the last session; and to provide for the cost of completing, equipping and operating the said railways-the operating expenses to be chargeable to revenue-revote, $3,667,745.07.
Will the minister explain this item?

It is a revote from last year. The vote last year was for $4,000,000. The difference between the two votes was spent on construction last year. We are trying to protect the road by putting in stone to prevent the current from washing out the ballast. Formerly, a quantity of timber and other material was put in the sides for that purpose.
This amount is not only for construction purposes, is it?
No.

What portion of the $3,667,745.07 will go towards the construction, what portion towards the payment of the bonds and what portion towards the equipment, appurtenances and properties in connection with these railways?

It is estimated it will cost $1,492,194 to finish the construction, of which $492,194 is the amount found for depreciation of the Saguenay railway. That is, it will take $1,000,000 to complete the construction, and $492,194 to take the place of the depreciation that has occurred.

How much of the
amount will go towards the price of the railways acquired by the Government?
Whatever Mr. Justice Cassels finds.

Mr. Justice Cassels ha= found already. Has he not given a judgment in that case? I have in my hand the reasons for judgment, and the matter is still before the courts, because I understand, by a hurried inquiry I made this morning, that an appeal has been lodged by the railway companies against the judgment of Mr. Justice Cassels.
There is an appeal in connection with the gas property which has nothing to do with this.
No, it is not included

I may have some comments to make on that later on. To proceed.
If on the other hand the value placed upon the Quebec, Montmorency and Charlevoix Railway is less than $2,500,000 then the difference between the value as ascertained and the $2,500,000 is to be deducted from any sums that may be found due in respect of the other two railways.
Sir Walter Cassels says further:
The agreement refers to it in the following language:
"It is understood and agreed by and between all the parties hereto jointly and severally that in case the Exchequer Court of Canada fixes the value of the line of railway and other property set out in schedule *C* hereto at a sum less than $2,500,000, the difference between the sum so fixed and the sum of $2,500,000 shall be deducted from the aggregate amount of the purchase price to be paid for the lines of railway and other properties set out in schedules 'B' and 'D' hereto.
"The intention of this agreement being that in no event shall His Majesty be liable to pay for the said three lines of railway and other properties a greater amount than the value thereof as fixed by the Exchequer Court less the sum of $2,500,000, the amount of the bonds to be assumed by His Majesty as aforesaid."
The judge explains that he takes it for granted that the various railway companies had good titles to the properties that were transferred to the Department of Railways. He also explains how he had arranged the proceedings before the Court, as follows:
I came to the conclusion that the only practical way of arriving at a result would be to adopt the method adopted in the arbitration in which I acted as counsel for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, in regard to what was known as the Onderdonk sections of the railway in British Columbia.
"He says further:
Competent experts were employed by the Crown to make a minute examination of the three lines of railway and to furnish in detail what they considered the proper amount to be deducted for depreciation. A large amount of time was occupied by these gentlemen in making this inquiry. Subsequently the railway companies, by their counsel, accepted as

correct the amounts as found by the experts for the Crown. The amount of the depreciation to be offset against the value of the railways has therefore been settled. The figures I will deal with later.
He says further:
Another question of considerable importance is in regard to the offset referred to in the statute as subsidies.
And he explains that he had to deduct from the actual value not only the federal subsidies but the provincial subsidies as well.
He also refused to allow interest during construction.
He allowed it during actual construction, but the Company claimed it during several years.
No.

The company was
claiming interest right along for several years.
I know, but we refused to allow it during oonistruotion. The witnesses admitted it would require three years to build the road.

Now, as to the account as filed toy the railways. As I have said, there are three railways, the Montmorency, the Quebec and Saguenay and the Lotbin-ifere and Megantic. The judge said:
I will deal first with that relating to the Montmorency division. The first item is dated July 1, 1898: road and equipment, real estate, buildings, etc., Montmorency division, $2,038,149.49. This starting point is assumed by the railways to have been the cost of construction up to that date. At the date in question, namely, the 1st July, 1898, according to Colonel Wurtele, the road had been constructed as far as Ste. Anne's. The mileage of this road was about 21 miles, and it may be that they were running a mile or two beyond. Even if it were granted that 22 miles instead of 21 miles of the railway had been constructed at that date, the cost would be in the neighborhood of $92,500 a mile. Colonel Wurtele puts it about $100,000. It seems a high figure. It is stated by counsel for the railway company that a certain portion of the right of way beyond Ste. Anne's had been procured. This may or may not be so. The proof before me is lacking on this point. Here there is a distinct difference between the views put forward by the counsel for the railway company, and the counsel for the Crown. The counsel for the railway company contend that what the court has to do, is to find the cost as if it were an accounting between the directors of the railway and its shareholders; and that this amount being shown by the books of the ' company as the amount expended at that date, should therefore be accepted as the cost. Numerous witnesses were called, gentlemen of good standing-accountants from Montreal- who gave evidence as to the custom in regard

to the charging up of interest, etc., to capital account.
When I deal with the case of the Saguenay Railway, the absurdity of this contention put forward on the part of the railway company will be apparent. The directors of a company might have to pay fifty per cent commission for obtaining a loan of a million dollars. It would undoubtedly be quite right as between themselves and their shareholders to charge this fifty per cent in their accounts. So also they might delay construction for a period of say 20 years, in the meanwhile paying interest on this bonded indebtedness. As between the directors and their shareholders, as a matter of book-keeping, it may be quite reasonable to charge up every item of expenditure. But the case before me is of a different character. I am not dealing with the accounts as between the shareholders and their directors. What I have to ascertain Is the value as between the vendor and the purchaser and that value must be the actual cost of the railways, less subsidies and less depreciation.
He goes on:
Now it is admitted that these two items of $500,000 referred to in schedule "A," and also the item of $794,869.58 floating liabilities, comprise part of this item of $2,038,149.40. Crown counsel in their statement were of opinion that these two items of $500,000 and $794,869.58 should be taken as the cost up to that date, namely July 1st, 1898. I do not agree with that contention. I fail to see how it can be assumed without further proof that the proceeds of these interim bonds, namely $500,000, went into the construction of the railway. They may or may not. That is a question of proof. The bonds were held by the various parties shown on page 15 as Schedule "A." They were held as collateral security by the various parties. What the nature of the debts due to these various parties is I would have thought susceptible of proof-at all events before such an item can be allowed, further inquiry will be necessary, and so with regard to the liabilities.
The judge put aside this first claim of $500,000.
It would be impossible to accept Colonel Wurtele's evidence as proving the fact that these two particular items went into the construction of the railway. Other evidence would be required before I would be willing to accept those two sums of $500,000 and $794,869.58 as having been expended in the construction of this 21 miles of railway.
So here are two items, totalling $1,294,869.58, which are put aside by the judge for good and valid reasons, and I would strongly object^to these two items reappearing in the Estimates and being paid to the company when it was understood last year, by the statute passed by thi6 Parliament, that the judge of the Exchequer Court would fix the amounts due to the railway companies for the actual value of the railways.
Do these two items reappear in the Estimates?
I do not know. The hon. gentleman does not say so.
We do not propose to pay anything unless the judge gives a verdict for it.

I have dealt now with
the two biggest items which are put aside by the judge of the Exchequer Court in the case of the Montmorency railway. To show the discrepancy between the experts of the company as to the ooet of construction, 1 shall call the attention of the oom-mitte to this remark made by the judge:
I may call the attention of counsel to the fact that in the trust deed, Schedule "D," at page 19, there is the estimate of cost of constructing certain extensions. The total is 11 miles-and the total estimate is $149,947, which would be under $14,000 a mile- and while of course the main railway previously built may not have been built at that low figure, the contrast between the two figures, namely, $92,500 a mile, and the $14,000 a mile, is striking.
It shows that there was lots of bookkeeping in the office of the company. Now he comes to the Lotbiniere and Megantic Railway, and says:
Dealing with the Megantic Railway the amount involved in connection with this railway is, comparatively speaking, not very large, hut I think that further proof of a similar nature to that suggested in regard to the Montmorency Railway should be forthcoming. The only evidence given is that of Mr. Robhins, the manager of the railway, and is mere surmise. He may or may not be correct when he states that it would1 probably cost about $11,000 a mile.
No direct evidence is adduced as to the actual cost of the construction of the railway. Now he comes to the Saguenay Railway, which is the third white elephant. He says:
Mr. Matthews, the manager of the railway, was called as a witness. He states that the construction of the Quebec and Saguenay Railway was started in April or May, 1911. Previous to that he believes exploration surveys were made. He points out that the main construction on this road stops some time about September, 1912, hut that certain small constructions were continued for quite awhile.
As I intend to make some extended remarks on this subject, we might as well call it six o'clock.
Progress reported.
On motion of Right Hon. Sir George Foster, the House adjourned at 6 p.m.
Monday, August 27, 1917.
